Nowicki and co‑workers investigated POCO graphite electrodes with grain sizes of 1 µm (AF‑5) and 10 µm (S‑180) on Hastelloy C‑22 and found that larger‑grained graphite gives higher process efficiency (higher MRR) but also higher relative tool wear, while smaller‑grained graphite yields the lowest surface roughness. (Nowicki et al. 2022)

A related study by Nowicki et al. frames the grain‑size issue as an industrial challenge and reports that fine‑grained graphite increases process efficiency and reduces tool wear; the authors also note that detached graphite grains affect discharge stability and process efficiency, and they provide empirical and mathematical models linking grain size and machining parameters to MRR, relative TWR, and Ra for negative polarity EDM of Hastelloy C‑22. (Nowicki et al. 2024)

These two experimental reports lead to a tension in the literature: one set of results associates larger graphite grains with higher MRR (at the cost of greater relative tool wear), while the other emphasizes improved efficiency and reduced wear with fine grains. Both studies, however, agree that discharge current and pulse duration are primary factors controlling MRR and Ra; additionally, one study identifies the time interval (pulse‑off time) as the dominant parameter governing relative wear of the graphite electrode. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Broader EDM literature on difficult‑to‑machine alloys reinforces the dominance of electrical parameters: Taguchi and ANOVA analyses in cryogenically treated superalloys and in titanium workpieces identify peak current (amperage) and pulse‑on time as the most influential factors for MRR, Ra and TWR. (Nas & Kara 2022)(Akıncıoğlu 2022) Ramabalan et al. specifically link current and pulse duration to pronounced electrode shape changes and wear when machining Hastelloy B2, reporting that unstable sparks and heat diffusion transform sharp electrode features into hemispherical ends. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

The EDM field recognises persistent challenges—high TWR, low MRR and elevated surface roughness—and reports multiple mitigation approaches such as cryogenic treatment, powder‑mixed dielectrics, ultrasonic assistance and coating methods; these association techniques are evaluated with respect to MRR, TWR, surface integrity and recast layer formation. (Shastri et al. 2022)(Sana et al. 2024)(Liew et al. 2020)

(Nowicki et al. 2022) Experimental comparisons using POCO graphite grades with grain sizes of 1 µm (AF-5) and 10 µm (S-180/EDM-180) report that finer-grained graphite reduces surface roughness while coarser grains increase material removal rate but also raise relative tool wear. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Multiple studies identify discharge current (peak current) and pulse-on time (pulse duration) as the principal electrical parameters that govern material removal rate and surface roughness in EDM. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nas & Kara 2022) Specifically, Taguchi and ANOVA analyses in a factorial design found peak current to explain the largest share of variation in both Ra and MRR in the tested superalloy samples. (Nas & Kara 2022) Other work similarly highlights current and pulse duration as dominant influences on electrode wear and the transformation of electrode geometry under unstable sparking conditions. (Ramabalan et al. 2024)

Mechanistically, studies link graphite grain size to discharge stability and removal efficiency: fine grains improve process stability and lower tool wear, whereas coarse grains detach and perturb the discharge, increasing both MRR and relative electrode depletion. (Nowicki et al. 2024) The experimental research on Hastelloy C-22 produced empirical and mathematical models that predict how machining parameters and graphite grain size interact to determine MRR, relative tool wear rate (TWR), and Ra. (Nowicki et al. 2022)(Nowicki et al. 2024)

Attempts to mitigate the key EDM limitations—high TWR, low MRR, and poor surface integrity—span several auxiliary methods, including cryogenic treatments, powder-mixed dielectrics, ultrasonic assistance, and hybrid process variants; reviews identify these approaches and note gaps where process physics and parametric sensitivity require further experimental and modelling work. (Nas & Kara 2022)

Despite detailed results for graphite electrodes on Hastelloy grades, the literature pins several gaps relevant to this thesis scope. Empirical evidence for copper electrodes, and for engineered composite electrodes comparing TWR and MRR directly against the graphite cases on Hastelloy, is not present in the supplied sources.

Selective Laser Melting (SLM) produces near-full-density metal parts by layerwise melting and fusion of powder with a high-power laser, a process that enables fabrication of complex geometries and has been widely applied to steels including maraging grades. (Yap et al. 2015)

As-built microstructures of SLM maraging steel are characteristically very fine and martensitic. One study reports submicron prior-austenite or martensitic features with an average size of about $0.31\ \mu$m, implying cooling rates on the order of $10^{7}\ \mathrm{K/s}$, and finds dense populations of needle-shaped nanoprecipitates of $ \mathrm{Ni_3X}$ (X = Ti, Al, Mo) within a martensitic matrix that account for age-hardening. (Tan et al. 2018) Another microstructural survey observed a fine-grained martensitic structure in as-printed maraging steel across multiple section orientations and detected no pronounced texture or anisotropy in the as-built microstructure. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)

The thermal history imposed by SLM acts as an intrinsic heat treatment: repeated thermal cycles during building drive in situ tempering, precipitation and other phase changes that distinguish AM microstructures from conventionally produced material. (Haghdadi et al. 2020) Subsequent deliberate heat treatments modify these as-built features: systematic aging increases nano-hardness and maximizes precipitation strengthening, while solution treatments and aging can influence residual stress, anisotropy and precipitate morphology. (Tan et al. 2018)(Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021) Combining thermochemical treatments with conventional heat treatments also alters surface compound layers and near-surface chemistry—plasma nitriding performed at $520\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$ for 6 h was studied both alone and following solution/aging steps to probe wear and corrosion responses. (Godec et al. 2021)

Reversion of martensite to austenite during intercritical tempering has been linked to both microstructural redistribution of alloying elements and electrochemical performance. One study tempered SLM maraging steel at an intercritical temperature ($720\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}$) and found that reversed austenite precipitated primarily along martensite-lath boundaries where local Ni enrichment from dissolved intermetallics promoted nucleation; the specimen with reversed austenite displayed a higher pitting potential, lower corrosion current density and a reduced corrosion rate in 3.5 wt% NaCl compared with as-printed, aged and homogenized counterparts. (Khan et al. 2022)

Surface state and near-surface microstructure also affect corrosion. Electropolishing reduced SLM maraging steel surface roughness by about 65%, and studies report that despite finer microstructure the corrosion behaviour of heat-treated SLM parts can be similar to that of conventionally wrought material, with precipitation state strongly influencing both hardness and electrochemical potential. (Ahmadkhaniha et al. 2021)(Tan et al. 2018)

Nitriding without prior aging produced defects in the compound nitride layer, whereas applying nitriding after prior heat treatments improved wear and corrosion resistance, indicating that prior microstructural state governs the success of thermochemical surface treatments. (Godec et al. 2021)

Household rooftop solar adoption is shaped by a mix of financial, informational, technical and institutional factors that operate together as motivators and inhibitors. Recent empirical research identifies government subsidies and financial considerations as primary motivators, while awareness, perceived technical risk and institutional barriers operate as important inhibitors. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Sovacool et al. 2022)

Upfront cost and finance emerge repeatedly as direct barriers to adoption. Survey-based studies find that capital cost and expectations about maintenance costs reduce willingness to adopt, with cost-related variables entering models as negative predictors of adoption or willingness-to-adopt. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Tanveer et al. 2021) Evidence from nationally representative household data in Uganda shows that affordability determines the type of solar technology adopted and that flexible payment mechanisms increase uptake among income-constrained households. (Aarakit et al. 2021) These findings indicate that both the absolute upfront price and the availability of payment options affect household investment decisions. (Aarakit et al. 2021)

Policy instruments—most notably subsidies—play a central role in shaping the economics of rooftop PV and thereby household decisions. Studies using behavioural and institutional frameworks identify PV subsidies as a primary motivator that reduces perceived initial investment risk and strengthens the financial case for households. (Parsad et al. 2020) National targets and policy commitments also structure deployment plans and signal government support for rooftop PV deployment. (Goel 2016)(J & Majid 2020) However, policy design and implementation challenges are noted as constraints on achieving stated national goals. (Goel 2016)

Awareness, knowledge and perceived technical barriers also figure prominently. Empirical models and forecasting exercises rank technical barriers and knowledge/awareness factors among significant predictors of household investment decisions in rooftop PV systems. (Parsad et al. 2020) Studies using theory-of-planned-behavior extensions report that perceived benefits, perceived risk and self-efficacy strongly influence willingness to adopt, with perceived risk and cost reducing uptake. (Tanveer et al. 2021) Local pilot-project surveys that include questions about users’ experience and space availability further document experiential and informational constraints at the consumer level. (Kappagantu et al. 2015)

Institutional and equity considerations affect who adopts and how policy interventions perform. Research highlights demographic and spatial inequities associated with household solar adoption and argues for attention to distributional outcomes when scaling rooftop PV. (Sovacool et al. 2022) Reviews of renewable-energy constraints emphasize that broader system-level obstacles—policy, regulatory and institutional capacity—hamper expansion even where resource potential exists. (Khare et al. 2013)(Kappagantu et al. 2015) Together, these studies suggest that addressing upfront affordability, improving information and risk perceptions, and resolving institutional implementation gaps are central to increasing household rooftop solar uptake. (Aarakit et al. 2021)(Parsad et al. 2020)

Household decisions about rooftop photovoltaic (PV) adoption are shaped by both financial and non‑financial factors identified across studies. Upfront cost and concerns about long‑term returns act as primary financial inhibitors: research using structural equation models found that lower prices and lower maintenance costs reduce apprehension about returns, while perceived cost negatively affects willingness to adopt. (Parsad et al. 2020)(Tanveer et al. 2021) Flexible payment mechanisms emerge as a practical way to address affordability constraints for income‑constrained households: evidence from Uganda shows that payment flexibility increases uptake of solar home systems and kits by enabling households to afford otherwise costly systems. (Aarakit et al. 2021)

Government subsidies and policy instruments play a dual role, both motivating adoption and shaping market growth. Subsidies operate as a leading motivator that mitigates initial investment risk and strengthens the environmental and financial rationale for PV investment, according to survey‑based work in India that combines SEM and ANN analyses. (Parsad et al. 2020) National targets and policy frameworks have explicitly prioritized rooftop PV within broader solar capacity goals, embedding rooftop deployment in planning documents and pilot programmes. (Goel 2016)(Kappagantu et al. 2015) At the same time, the literature reviewing India’s renewable sector notes a range of obstacles that persist despite pro‑renewable policy intent, indicating gaps between policy design and on‑the‑ground uptake. (J & Majid 2020)

Knowledge, technical capacity, and perceived risk form important non‑financial barriers. Studies identify awareness, technical barriers, and knowledge gaps as significant predictors of household investment decisions, with technical constraints and limited consumer understanding reducing the likelihood of adoption. (Parsad et al. 2020) Perceived risk and doubts about technology effectiveness also lower willingness to adopt, as shown in multi‑city household surveys that extended the theory of planned behaviour. (Tanveer et al. 2021) Pilot projects that surveyed consumers about roof space, consumption patterns, and user experience highlight practical implementation concerns that can impede deployment even where policy support exists. (Kappagantu et al. 2015)

Equity and spatial heterogeneity further complicate barriers to rooftop PV. Analyses of global household solar adoption identify demographic and spatial inequities—between groups and across geographies—that can lead to uneven distribution of benefits and risks as deployment scales.
